home_seo_desc: Qingjian is a pinyin input method for macOS written in Rust. Each candidate carries a gloss in English or Japanese, so you pick up a word while you type. Sentence input, double pinyin, fuzzy pinyin and spelling correction, all on your device, with no data uploaded.
home_intro_1: Qingjian is a pinyin input method written in Rust. It converts whole sentences, and a small on-device model reorders the candidates.
home_intro_2: As you type, each candidate carries a gloss in the language you are learning. No interruptions, no pop-up quizzes.
home_handwritten_2: pick up a word on the way.
home_demo_label: Demo of the candidate window while typing qingjian
benefit_local_desc: Pinyin, dictionaries, sentence model, learning and glosses all work offline
benefit_gloss_desc: Part of speech + English or Japanese, one language at a time
benefit_fresh_desc: Glosses you've rarely seen are orange until they feel familiar
benefit_better_desc: Word frequency, your own phrasing and your typos are learned on-device
home_features_title: An input method has to be a good input method first
home_features_desc: Language learning is built on top of that. If you ever have to ask yourself "am I typing or studying vocabulary right now?", Qingjian got the design wrong.
feature_input_desc: Sentence conversion (an on-device model reorders candidates), abbreviated pinyin, spelling correction, fuzzy pinyin, double pinyin, English mode and emoji. Typing speed never gives way to learning.
feature_gloss_title: Part of speech + gloss, one per candidate
feature_gloss_desc: The bundled glossary covers the whole dictionary. Choose English or Japanese; Japanese glosses carry kana readings above the kanji. Languages are never stacked side by side.
feature_personal_desc: The words you pick, the sequences you pick them in and the typo fixes you accept are remembered on-device, and sentence conversion and ranking adapt to them.
feature_cloud_title: Optional cloud suggestions, off by default
feature_cloud_desc: Once enabled, Qingjian asks the AI provider you set up for words and sentence completions as you type. It can also explain characters and translate selected text.
home_example_title: Candidates come first; the gloss is smaller and quieter
home_example_desc: Candidates for kaifa with Chinese as the main language. You choose the learning language in Settings, and there is only one at a time.
home_example_note: Orange marks a new word: this gloss has been in the candidate window fewer than three times when you committed text. Once it's familiar it turns grey on its own, with no icons and no pop-ups. Japanese glosses carry hiragana over each kanji.
home_nongoals_desc: Qingjian isn't trying to become an all-in-one language-learning app.
nongoal_languages: Cram five or six languages into the candidate window
nongoal_quiz: Pop up a quiz every few words
nongoal_ui: Get in the way of typing with a complicated UI
nongoal_speed: Trade typing speed for learning features

about_seo_desc: Where the name Qingjian comes from, the idea of "typing first, learning on the side", how the engine turns a keystroke into candidates on your device, platform status, the license and where the bundled data comes from.
about_title: Typing first, learning on the side.
about_desc: Qingjian is a pinyin input method written in Rust. Its goal isn't only to turn pinyin into Chinese characters, but to make typing itself a light, continuous and nearly effortless way to meet another language.
about_name_p1: A jian (简) is a bamboo or wooden slip that ancient Chinese texts were written on; slips bound together became books. Qingjian, "green slips", has long been used to mean books, classics and written records.
about_name_p2: The name keeps a sense of Chinese writing culture without tying the input method to any one language in the future. Qingjian is for Chinese writers first, but it doesn't plan to be a Chinese-only input method forever.
about_idea_p1: Chatting, coding, searching, taking notes, writing documents, sending email: we spend a huge share of our time typing. If those hundreds of daily keystrokes could give a little language feedback along the way, learning would stop being something you set time aside for and become part of your day.
about_idea_p2_a: Type as usual, and pick up a word along the way. No interruptions, no quizzes, no forced memorization — the gloss just sits quietly beside the candidate.
about_idea_p2_c: : each candidate gets a single gloss, never English, Japanese, Korean and German all at once.
about_flow_title: The path of a keystroke through the engine
about_flow_desc: Every step below runs on your device with no network. Cloud suggestions are an optional extra outside this pipeline.
about_core_title: Platforms are just shells; the core is Qingjian
about_core_desc: Dictionaries, pinyin parsing, candidate generation, ranking, learning and glosses all live in a platform-independent core. The macOS, Windows and Linux shells do only two things: turn system keystrokes into input for the core, and draw the candidates it returns in a window. Swap IMK for TSF and not a single line of the core changes.
about_fast_desc: Glosses come from a local table; candidates appear first and glosses are drawn in afterwards. Any delay, pop-up or visual distraction added for the sake of learning counts as a design bug. The target is under 10 ms per keystroke, and most keystrokes measure 1 to 3 ms.
about_safe_desc: Learning data and settings are written to a temporary file, flushed to disk and then renamed, so the disk always holds either the old file or the new one. Damaged lines are skipped without stopping startup. Unexpected errors inside the input method are caught at the boundary, and the letters you were typing are passed to the app untouched.
about_platforms_desc: The core engine is platform-independent; macOS comes first in development.
about_license_section_desc: The macOS beta and the Windows alpha are both available for download; the installers aren't developer-signed yet. The code is open source.
about_license_p1_a: The code is open source under GPL-3.0-or-later: you may use, modify and redistribute it freely, and modified versions you distribute must be open source too. The Qingjian name and logo aren't covered by the license. The source code is on
about_license_p2: Qingjian is free through its official channels. If you paid someone to get it, you were scammed.
about_data_title: Where the bundled data comes from
about_data_desc: Each source follows its own license; the same list appears on the About page in Settings.
data_dict_src: Table of General Standard Chinese Characters; Lexicon of Common Words in Contemporary Chinese (liuxilu's proofread edition); THUOCL topic words (Tsinghua University NLP Lab, MIT); readings from Unihan (Unicode License v3)
data_lm_src: Statistics from Chinese Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) and LCCC (Tsinghua University CoAI, MIT)
data_gloss_src: Generated offline with a large language model (DeepSeek); built by Qingjian
data_english_src: ESDB / SCOWL (© Kevin Atkinson); CSpell dictionaries (MIT)
data_levels_src: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Yukio Tono); Octanove Vocabulary Profile C1/C2 (CC BY-SA 4.0); JLPT word lists (tanos.co.uk, CC BY; compiled by elzup/jlpt-word-list, MIT)
privacy_seo_desc: Qingjian uploads no data: pinyin conversion, dictionaries, learning and glosses all stay on your device. Cloud suggestions are off by default, and the input log is written only locally and can be turned off or cleared at any time. Here's exactly which files exist and how to remove them all.
privacy_title: It gets to know you. No server needs to.
privacy_desc: Qingjian uploads no data. Pinyin conversion, dictionaries, learning and glosses all happen on your device. No account, no usage reporting.
principle_account_desc: No sign-up, no sign-in, no usage statistics
principle_local_desc: Pinyin conversion, dictionaries, learning and glosses work offline
principle_cloud_desc: When on, data goes only to the provider you set up
privacy_sources_title: Only two things produce data, and both are in your hands
privacy_sources_desc: One is off by default, one is on by default; each can be switched off in one click.
privacy_cloud_p_a: Once enabled, the pinyin you're typing, a few dozen characters of context on either side of the cursor and the local candidates are sent to the AI provider you entered on the 云服务 (Cloud services) page in Settings — DeepSeek by default, or any OpenAI-compatible API. Data goes straight from your computer to that provider and
privacy_cloud_p_c: : Qingjian has no servers of its own.
privacy_cloud_li1: Nothing is ever sent from password fields (Secure Input).
privacy_cloud_li2: While it's on, a word with no gloss in the bundled glossary is sent once on its own after you type it — just that word. The returned gloss is saved to your personal glossary on this device, where you can edit it.
privacy_cloud_li3: A ☁︎ after 中 / 英 in the menu bar means suggestions are on. Turn off the switch on the 云服务 (Cloud services) page and no more requests are sent.
privacy_log_p_a: Each time you commit text, one line is written on this device: the keys you pressed, how they were segmented, the top candidates you saw and which one you picked. It holds only keystrokes and committed text, never context from the app. It stays in this computer's data folder for offline evaluation and your own personal model, and
privacy_log_p_b: is never sent to anyone automatically
privacy_log_li1: Turn it off: on the 高级 (Advanced) page in Settings, uncheck 记录输入日志 (Record input log).
privacy_log_li2: Clear it: 清空输入日志 (Clear input log) on the same page.
privacy_log_li3: If you're willing to send this file to the author during testing, it helps a lot with ranking — but it's entirely up to you.
privacy_files_title: Which files are on your device
privacy_files_desc: All in ~/Library/Application Support/Qingjian/, as plain text you can open any time.
file_env: Cloud service keys, only if you entered any; readable only by your user account
file_user: How many times each word was picked
file_user_words: Automatically created words and user words picked from the cloud
file_user_choices: Which word you picked for a given pinyin
file_user_english: English words you committed as typed
file_user_typos: Typo corrections you accepted (what you typed and what you meant)
file_user_ngram: Which word tends to follow which
file_user_glossary: Personal glosses filled in from the cloud
file_user_vocab: How often each gloss was seen / committed / typed
file_usage: Daily counts of characters, words and commits — numbers only
file_input_log: Input log: keys, segmentation, candidates and the pick for each commit
privacy_files_note: The character and vocabulary counts on the 统计 (Statistics) page in Settings come from usage.tsv and user-vocab.tsv, not from the input log: turn the log off or clear it and the statistics remain. These files are replaced whole each time, so even if the input method crashes it never leaves a half-written file.
privacy_logs_desc: Only what's needed to troubleshoot, nothing more.
privacy_runlog_a: Stored in ~/Library/Logs/Qingjian/, one file per day, kept for 7 days. The default level
privacy_runlog_c: . Only when you turn on 详细日志 (Verbose logging) on the 高级 (Advanced) page is each keystroke logged, for troubleshooting — remember to turn it off afterwards.
privacy_diag_a: This button on the 关于 (About) page copies the version, system, loaded data, raw settings and log folder to the clipboard; you decide whether to send it. Sending it to the author helps pin problems down faster.
privacy_delete_desc: All data lives in files on your device. Once deleted, it's gone — there are no cloud copies.
privacy_delete_li1: To clear only the input log: 清空输入日志 (Clear input log) on the 高级 (Advanced) page in Settings.
privacy_delete_li2_a: To remove the input method together with its data, run
privacy_delete_li2_c: it uninstalls the input method but keeps your learning data.
privacy_delete_li3_a: Imported dictionaries are in the data folder's
privacy_delete_li3_b: ; "Remove" in Settings only moves them to
privacy_delete_li3_c: , so clear that folder yourself to delete them for good.

themes_desc: Give the candidate window a new look. Download a theme, put it in the themes folder inside your data folder and pick it in Settings; it looks the same on macOS and Windows.
themes_contribute_a: A theme is a folder with theme.json, a README and a few screenshots. See the
themes_contribute_b: for the format. You can start from the built-in Sakura theme, then open a PR on the themes repository.

theme_install_c: inside your data folder, then pick it under 设置 → 候选窗口 → 主题 (Settings → Candidate window → Theme).
theme_builtin_note: This theme ships with Qingjian. Just pick "{name}" under 设置 → 候选窗口 → 主题 (Settings → Candidate window → Theme); no download needed.
